paragraphs: The core transaction for occupational therapists is turning the dressing, meal preparation, study, or work activity that the client wants to do again into observable barriers and goals, then restoring safe participation through training, assistive devices, and environmental adjustment.

The more favorable signals are: you are willing to patiently observe a real activity, ask what outcome the client truly cares about, record small changes, and keep watching for safety in close-range collaboration.

What calls for caution: this is not just writing plans in an office. Clinical settings may require helping someone stand, transferring them, and handling slow progress and emotional frustration, while adjusting goals without crossing safety and qualification boundaries.

First do a 45—60 minute safe trial: use the fictional bedside-to-washbasin scenario to map the steps, mark two barriers, deliver one environmental adjustment and one step-by-step exercise, and then check whether you enjoy repeated observation, recording, and revision.
Occupational therapists correspond to O*NET-SOC 29-1122.00, focusing on whether the client can safely and meaningfully complete activities of daily living, learning, work, and social participation.

entries: Through history, interview, and actual task observation, identify whether physical function, cognition, the environment, or task steps limit occupational performance.
Set measurable goals with the client and turn dressing, handwriting, meal preparation, or return-to-work tasks into purposeful activity training.
Select and teach the use of assistive devices, and adjust placement, signage, and processes at home, school, or the workplace to reduce activity barriers.

paragraphs: Work settings may be hospitals, outpatient clinics, schools, residential care facilities, or the client's home; deliverables include assessment records, goals, intervention plans, progress notes, and home guidance.

The key judgment is not whether the movement can be completed, but which barrier most affects the client's goal and what training, device, or environmental change can safely change actual participation.

Occupational therapists are not the same as physical therapists or rehabilitation counselors; their central responsibility is activity analysis, functional goals, activity intervention, and environmental adaptation.

O*NET shows that this occupation simultaneously requires face-to-face communication, recording information, decision-making and problem solving, caring for others, and collaborating with the medical team; it is not a purely manual-technique role.

Occupational therapists support clients in completing meaningful activities such as daily living, learning, and work; physical therapists focus more on motor function and pain, while this occupation's output is activity participation.
The comparison is based on BLS/O*NET occupational duties; U.S. licensure and Chinese post conditions must both be verified separately, and the name rehabilitation cannot be used interchangeably.
Choose from the deliverables you enjoy: activity analysis and environmental adaptation, motor function training, speech and communication, resource coordination, or assistive devices.
Compared with physical therapists, occupational therapists place movement ability into specific activity goals such as dressing, washing, meal preparation, and returning to school.

If you prefer turning life tasks into measurable goals and repeatedly adjusting the environment, you can deepen in occupational therapy; if you prefer exercise prescription, verify physical therapy qualifications separately.
Preparing explorers
Use a fictional washing task to practice observation, goals, and safety boundaries; real treatment requires compliant training.
Practicing therapists
Let AI organize record drafts, while treatment goals, contraindications, effects, and the medical record are verified by the therapist.
Clinical preceptors
Review tool omissions, privacy, and erroneous suggestions, and preserve the trainee's actual activity observation.
Institution managers
First set data permissions, the professional reviewer, and the error escalation process, then evaluate tool use.

paragraphs: After the trial, record separately: whether you saw a concrete barrier, whether the suggestion is executable, whether you considered falls and over-assistance, and whether you are willing to collect feedback and redo a version.

Different settings put different demands on you: pediatric and school settings emphasize activity design and home-school communication, while inpatient and geriatric services more often involve transfer, assistive devices, and caregiver training.
Real treatment follows local licensure, institutional procedures, and professional responsibility; a paper case does not grant patient assessment or treatment authority.
Transfer falls, wrong goals, medical record privacy, and ill-fitting assistive devices can all harm the client; identify, escalate, document, and re-evaluate according to team procedures.
Based on BLS occupational therapy tasks, AOTA AI ethics policy, NBCOT education accreditation, and applicable state regulation; different jurisdictions must not be mixed.
Clients, caregivers, occupational therapists, and the medical team.
Assisting a transfer without assessing weight-bearing and the environment may cause a fall or strain; re-assess and select staffing and assistance measures according to institutional procedures.

The United States usually requires a master's degree in occupational therapy and a state license; NBCOT examination eligibility, certification, and state licensure are separate. Chinese rehabilitation therapy post conditions are verified against the specific institution and local rules.

Fictional case: an adult wants to complete morning washing independently; the given observations are three items: the countertop is too high, supplies are scattered, and completing the steps requires prompting. First list facts, unknowns, safety constraints, and observable goals; do not diagnose disease or use a real medical record.
Activity observation

Reference delivery: write a washing step diagram and two barriers to verify, propose one environmental placement adjustment and one step-by-step exercise, and state the stop conditions and the matters that must be handed to a qualified team for review.
Goal design

Seven-day paper experience: read the tasks, list activity steps, separate observation from guessing, write goals, compare adjustments, simulate recording feedback, and reflect on interest. The portfolio contains the fictional inputs, goals, risk stop conditions, and review plan.
Safe implementation

The competence stages are only an editorial suggestion: from accurate observation, to designing measurable goals, to safe implementation and cross-scenario re-evaluation; real treatment authority follows the jurisdiction, qualifications, and institutional procedures and is not automatically obtained through years of service or a paper portfolio.

Chinese and U.S. entry rules are verified separately: a single Shanghai recruitment sample is not a uniform national education requirement, and NBCOT certification does not equal a license in every state.

career_risk_cards.heading: Safety and responsibility risks in occupational therapy

risks.mitigation: First assess weight-bearing and the environment, and arrange staffing and devices per institutional procedure.
risks.scenario: Assisting standing or transfer without verifying ability.
risks.title: Transfer falls

risks.consequence: The intervention may drift from the client's participation goals, making progress hard to explain or requiring a new plan.
risks.mitigation: Negotiate observable goals and re-evaluate regularly.
risks.scenario: Applying a fixed training routine without asking the client's goals.
risks.title: Unsuitable goals

risks.consequence: Ill-fitting size or environment may increase falls, pain, or barriers to use.
risks.mitigation: Trial on site and verify the environment and use training.
risks.scenario: Recommending grab bars or devices without trialing them.
risks.title: Ill-fitting assistive devices

risks.consequence: Identifiable health information may be disclosed, harming privacy and trust.
risks.mitigation: Follow institutional minimum-necessary, access, and audit rules.
risks.scenario: Entering identifiable medical records into an unapproved tool.
risks.title: Privacy disclosure

risks.affected_roles: Clients, the treatment team, and successor personnel
risks.consequence: Missing pain, fatigue, and activity changes may delay plan adjustment and risk escalation.
risks.mitigation: Document, hand over, and escalate abnormalities promptly.
risks.scenario: Not recording pain, fatigue, or activity changes after training.
risks.title: Missing change records

risks.affected_roles: Clients, interns, supervising therapists, and institutions
risks.consequence: Unauthorized conclusions may cause improper intervention, unclear responsibility, and inaccurate records.
risks.mitigation: Reviewed and signed by authorized personnel.
risks.scenario: An intern or tool draft is treated as a formal management conclusion.
risks.title: Signing beyond authority
